set1.q: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a car crash with a heart rate of 128 and a blood pressure of 88/56. The rhythm is regular with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Bedside ultrasound shows free fluid in the abdomen. Which is the most appropriate approach to her heart rate?
opts: Adenosine is for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; a sinus tachycardia compensating for blood loss settles when the cause is treated.
Cardioversion cannot fix a compensatory sinus rhythm and would not restore her volume; the cause must be treated.
Slowing a compensatory tachycardia in a hypovolemic patient would remove her compensation; the bleeding is what needs treatment.
Correct. This is appropriate sinus tachycardia from hypovolemia, a pathologic cause; management of appropriate sinus tachycardia is treating the underlying cause.

Her heart rate is 172 and regular, with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three or more P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; her rhythm is regular, which points to nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding
Sinus tachycardia shows a normal P wave before each QRS and rarely exceeds 160; hers has hidden P waves at 172 with sudden onset.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A paroxysmal, regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves, neck pulsations (the frog sign) and a stimulant trigger in a young woman without heart disease is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia.

The electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Procainamide is reserved for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; a stable narrow complex tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.
Correct. A stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia above 160 with hidden P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and the first-line treatment when stable is a vagal maneuver, then adenosine.
Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver fails.
Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.

opts: Sinus tachycardia has a normal P wave before each QRS, not two sawtooth waves per QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three or more distinct P-wave shapes, not uniform sawtooth waves.
Correct. Sawtooth flutter waves with two for every narrow QRS are atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the most common ratio, and atrial scarring after surgery is a classic setting.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no organized atrial waves; his rhythm is regular with sawtooth waves.

set1.q: A 77-year-old man had cardiac surgery last year. A rhythm strip shows normal sinus beats, then a sudden pause with no P wave that is not a multiple of the preceding P-P interval, after which narrow beats at 45 appear with no visible P waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia is a normal breathing-linked variation with a P wave before every beat, never a pause followed by junctional beats.
Atrial flutter shows rapid sawtooth waves at 250 or more, not a pause followed by slow narrow beats without P waves.

Correct. In sinus arrest the sinus node fails to generate an impulse, so the pause is not a multiple of the P-P interval and a junctional rhythm (narrow beats without visible P waves) may take over; surgical injury to the node is a listed cause.

In exit block the impulse is generated but cannot leave the node, so the pause is typically an exact multiple of the P-P interval; a pause that is not a multiple points to sinus arrest, where the node fails to fire.

opts: Infrequent, asymptomatic beats need nothing, but frequent ones prompt a search for structural heart disease.
Correct. If premature atrial contractions are frequent, look for underlying structural heart disease; in a diseased heart they may precede supraventricular tachycardia, fibrillation or flutter.
An accessory pathway is suspected with a short PR and delta wave; frequent premature atrial beats prompt a structural workup.
Digoxin toxicity is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, not of frequent premature atrial beats; frequent premature atrial contractions prompt a search for structural heart disease.

opts: Myectomy treats obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it has no role in premature atrial beats.
Correct. Catheter ablation is used if premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; premature beats triggering fibrillation are targeted by ablation.
Carotid surgery treats carotid artery stenosis; premature atrial beats that trigger fibrillation are ablated.

opts: Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred when anticoagulation is needed; his low score may not require it.
A heparin infusion is not an outpatient plan; with a score of 0, anticoagulation may not be needed.
Correct. A CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score of 0 in a man (or 1 in a woman) is low risk and may not require anticoagulation.
Warfarin targets an international normalized ratio of 2 to 3 when anticoagulation is needed; a score of 0 in a man is low risk.

set1.q: A 19-year-old woman with Wolff-Parkinson-White has had three emergency visits for reentrant tachycardia this year. Which long-term management is first line?
opts: Adenosine is intravenous, acts for seconds and is dangerous in pre-excited atrial fibrillation; it cannot be long-term therapy.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms and does not stop conduction down an accessory pathway.
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation; it does not treat the accessory pathway.
Correct. Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is first-line chronic management of Wolff-Parkinson-White, removing the substrate for reentry and pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

opts: Correct. Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation prevents stroke; the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score is used to assess that risk, which rises with age.
Anticoagulants do not affect conduction; their purpose in atrial fibrillation is preventing stroke.
Anticoagulants do not prevent ventricular arrhythmias; they prevent embolic stroke.
Rate control drugs, not anticoagulants, slow the heart; anticoagulants prevent stroke.

opts: Correct. When atropine fails in acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, the next step is a temporary pacemaker; a permanent pacemaker follows if the cause will not resolve.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node and would slow him further; after failed atropine, a temporary pacemaker is used.
A synchronized shock is for unstable fast rhythms; a slow rhythm unresponsive to atropine needs temporary pacing.
A beta blocker is a cause of bradycardia, not a rescue for it; the next step after atropine is a temporary pacemaker.

set1.q: A 24-year-old man is told his electrocardiogram shows a normal P wave before each narrow QRS at 68 beats per minute, with the rate rising as he breathes in and falling as he breathes out. He worries that he has heart disease. Which counseling is most accurate?
opts: Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; sinus arrhythmia carries no clot risk and needs no treatment.
Correct. A sinus rate that speeds with inspiration and slows with expiration, with normal P waves and a narrow QRS, is sinus arrhythmia, a normal physiologic variant that needs no treatment.
Pacemakers are for symptomatic bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome or high-grade block; a breathing-linked sinus variation is normal and needs nothing.
Exercise restriction has no place here; sinus arrhythmia is a normal physiologic response to breathing.

opts: Ventricular tachycardia can occur in some patients, who then need a defibrillator with the pacemaker, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
A junctional rhythm is a slow escape rhythm (usually 40 to 60), not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome the tachyarrhythmia that alternates with bradycardia or pauses is most commonly atrial fibrillation.
Flutter is an organized atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; it is not the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.

opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; she is stable, so rate control comes first.
Adenosine is used for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; flutter at 140 needs rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
A beta or calcium channel blocker
Correct. Hemodynamically stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; rate control is the first goal, though harder to achieve than in fibrillation.

Sinus bradycardia keeps an upright, normal P wave before each QRS; his are inverted or buried.
ruled out by a stated finding

Observation suits an asymptomatic healthy person; a symptomatic junctional rhythm from high-grade block needs a pacemaker.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node further and would worsen the high-grade block causing his rhythm.

Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia is treated first with atropine; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent one.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.
Synchronized cardioversion is a timed shock for an unstable tachycardia with a pulse; unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine first.

opts: Correct. Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, and her weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation point to it, so thyroid testing comes next.
Digoxin causes bradycardia, but she takes no medications; her symptoms point to hypothyroidism instead.
ruled out by a stated finding

Monitoring for pauses suits suspected sick sinus syndrome; her symptoms suggest hypothyroidism, checked first with thyroid tests.

opts: A beta blocker is for persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions after triggers are addressed, not the first response.
Ablation is for frequent premature atrial contractions or those triggering atrial fibrillation; hers are occasional and benign.
Anticoagulation is for atrial fibrillation and flutter; isolated premature atrial beats need none.
Correct. Premature atrial contractions in a normal heart with excess alcohol, stress or caffeine are benign: counsel avoidance of precipitants and reassure about the benign nature of the rhythm.

Older age raises stroke risk rather than ruling out anticoagulation; a high score means she typically needs it.
Correct. Direct oral anticoagulants (dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) are preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation; a high stroke-risk score means she needs anticoagulation.

Magnesium is the drug for torsades de pointes; stable focal atrial tachycardia gets a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Correct. Stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia is treated with an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker while the underlying cause is identified and treated.

opts: Atropine is a short-acting rescue for acute unstable bradycardia, not long-term protection against pauses.
Ablation does nothing for the failing sinus node that causes his pauses; he needs a permanent pacemaker.
Observation is appropriate only when symptoms do not correlate with the bradycardia; his fainting during pauses needs a pacemaker.
Correct. When symptoms correlate with bradycardia in sick sinus syndrome a permanent pacemaker is placed, and tachy-brady syndrome often needs one.

opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but keeps P waves, in at least three shapes; his tracing has none.
ruled out by a stated finding

ruled out by a stated finding
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a normal P wave before every beat at 60 to 100; he has no P waves at 132.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. An irregularly irregular narrow complex rhythm with absent P waves is atrial fibrillation, and hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea and older age are listed risk factors.

The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Adenosine is contraindicated here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway carry the fibrillation.
Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a long QT, not pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Atropine speeds conduction and is for unstable bradycardia; it would accelerate a pre-excited tachycardia.
Correct. Irregular, wide, very fast complexes in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White are pre-excited atrial fibrillation, treated with intravenous procainamide; adenosine must never be used.

opts: Correct. Medical emergencies from atrial fibrillation include severe heart failure (pulmonary edema, hypotension) and atrial fibrillation with an acute myocardial infarction.
A rate above 100 is rapid ventricular response, which needs rate control but is not by itself the listed emergency.
An irregularly irregular pulse defines atrial fibrillation and is not itself the emergency.
Older age raises atrial fibrillation risk but does not make a presentation an emergency; severe heart failure does.

opts: Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; it does not treat a focal atrial tachycardia.
Correct. Catheter ablation of the ectopic focus is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia (about 90%), after oral beta blockers or calcium channel blockers as initial therapy.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; an ectopic atrial focus driving a tachycardia is cured by ablation.
Adenosine usually fails to terminate focal atrial tachycardia and has no long-term role.

opts: Correct. Hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia (hypotension and confusion) gets immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage.
A vagal maneuver is first line only for the stable patient; hypotension with confusion calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion.
Adenosine is for the stable patient after a vagal maneuver; this patient is unstable and needs synchronized cardioversion.

opts: Correct. A slow regular narrow rhythm with inverted P waves after the QRS is a junctional rhythm, and digoxin toxicity is a listed cause.
Hyperthyroidism speeds the sinus node; it does not produce a slow junctional rhythm.
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation and fast reentry, not a slow junctional rhythm.
Missing doses lowers the digoxin effect rather than slowing the heart further; nausea and fatigue with a slow junctional rhythm point to digoxin toxicity, a listed cause.

No urgent care is usually needed
Correct. If a vagal maneuver terminates nodal reentry in a patient who has been educated, urgent medical attention is usually not required.
An emergency visit is not needed once an educated patient has terminated the episode and feels well.

opts: Correct. Fast rhythms alternating with bradycardia and offset pauses are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome in which the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation.
Ventricular fibrillation is a pulseless arrest rhythm, not a recurring run she survives; the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome is atrial fibrillation.
In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.
Nodal reentry is a regular narrow tachycardia, usually in younger women without heart disease; it is not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation started an antiarrhythmic and then develops atrial flutter. Suddenly her ventricular rate matches her atrial rate at 280, with hypotension. Which complication is she now at high risk of?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregular atrial rhythm of lung disease; the danger of 1:1 flutter is ventricular fibrillation.
Correct. 1:1 atrial flutter, where every flutter wave conducts, causes extreme hemodynamic instability and carries a big risk of progression to ventricular fibrillation.
With 1:1 conduction the ventricular rate is as fast as the atrial rate, not slow; the danger is extreme hemodynamic instability and progression to ventricular fibrillation.
Sinus arrest is a failure of the sinus node to fire, part of sick sinus syndrome, not the danger of 1:1 flutter.

A pacemaker is not a prerequisite for cardioversion; three weeks of anticoagulation is.
Rate control continues; the requirement before elective cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation.

Myectomy relieves outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it does not treat flutter.
Carotid surgery treats carotid stenosis; recurrent flutter is referred for catheter ablation.
Correct. Ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter, which has a substantial recurrence rate and is harder to rate-control than fibrillation.

set2.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A normal P wave before every narrow QRS at 60 to 100, with the rate rising on inspiration and falling on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia: a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern.
Sick sinus syndrome produces pauses, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings in a diseased node, usually with symptoms; a breathing-linked variation in a healthy swimmer is sinus arrhythmia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast, irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients; her single P-wave shape at 72 is sinus.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; she has a normal P wave before every beat and a regular pattern tied to breathing.

opts: A pacemaker is for junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome, not an asymptomatic athlete.
Atropine is for acute, unstable, symptomatic bradycardia; he is an asymptomatic, healthy athlete.
Training explains his high vagal tone and is not harmful here; he needs no treatment.
Correct. A junctional rhythm can be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as well-conditioned athletes, and needs no treatment when asymptomatic in an otherwise healthy person.

set2.q: A 31-year-old woman has inappropriate sinus tachycardia at about 110 after a full workup excluded other causes. Her only symptom is awareness of her heartbeat, and she asks whether she needs medication. Which response is most accurate?
opts: She needs a lifelong beta blocker
Beta blockers are not well tolerated in inappropriate sinus tachycardia, which is why it is usually left untreated.
Cardioversion resets reentrant or fibrillatory rhythms; inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm and is usually left untreated.
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; a sinus tachycardia carries no such need.

Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is generally left untreated: patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment, beta blockers are poorly tolerated, and the prognosis is usually benign.

Correct. If warfarin is used for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation, the target international normalized ratio is 2 to 3.
A target of 3.5 to 4.5 is higher than needed and raises bleeding risk; atrial fibrillation targets 2 to 3.

A vagal maneuver fails, and adenosine slows the rate to reveal an irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, each with a delta wave (slurred upstroke). Which is the next step?
opts: Atropine speeds conduction and treats unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster.
An oral beta blocker is too slow and, as a nodal blocker, leaves the accessory pathway unopposed; procainamide is the drug used.

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is never repeated: nodal blockade leaves the accessory pathway unopposed.
More adenosine blocks only the normal node, leaving the accessory pathway free to conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.

Adenosine acts for seconds to stop reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; it cannot suppress premature beats.
Warfarin is an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation; it does nothing for premature atrial beats.

opts: Sinus arrhythmia is a normal breathing-linked variation in the sinus rate and poses no danger to him.
Correct. Atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway is the most dangerous combination: it can exceed 200, approaching 300, and cause collapse.
Sinus tachycardia is a normal response to exercise and conducts through the normal system at rates up to 160.
Isolated premature atrial beats are usually benign; the dangerous rhythm is atrial fibrillation conducting down the pathway.

opts: Procainamide is the drug of choice for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not one to avoid.
Cardioversion is appropriate if she becomes unstable; the treatment to avoid is adenosine.
Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line chronic treatment for Wolff-Parkinson-White.

Correct. In atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, adenosine must never be used: blocking the normal atrioventricular node leaves the accessory pathway to conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.

opts: Sinus tachycardia keeps the patient's normal P-wave shape; a consistent abnormal P wave means an ectopic atrial focus.
ruled out by a stated finding
Flutter shows sawtooth waves at 250 or more per minute, not a single abnormal P wave before each QRS at 160.

Correct. A regular tachycardia with one consistent, abnormally shaped P wave before each QRS, starting abruptly in someone without heart disease under increased metabolic demand, is focal atrial tachycardia.

opts: A vagal maneuver is the first-line step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, not something to avoid.
Adenosine is the second step after a failed vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia.
Adenosine may be given twice as needed in stable supraventricular tachycardia, so a second dose is appropriate.

Correct. Unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; a stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine, and only an unstable one with synchronized cardioversion.

opts: An extra pathway causing fast rhythms
Correct. Pre-excitation with a delta wave means an accessory pathway (the bundle of Kent), which carries the potential for reentrant tachycardia, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White.
A sign of a prior heart attack
Infarction changes the ST segment and Q waves; a short PR with a delta wave reflects an accessory pathway.
Athletic hearts show sinus bradycardia or junctional rhythm; a delta wave is an accessory pathway, not training.
A slow node needing a pacemaker
Pre-excitation speeds conduction to the ventricles through an extra pathway; it is not a slow node that needs pacing.

Atropine is first line only for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; a well, conditioned runner needs no drug.

Duration alone is not the threshold given; collapse usually needs a rate above 200.

Correct. Supraventricular tachycardia usually does not cause syncope or hemodynamic collapse unless the rate goes above 200, as in reentry tachycardias or atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway.
Above 100 is simply tachycardia; collapse from supraventricular tachycardia usually needs a rate above 200.
Older age can make symptoms more pronounced, but collapse is tied to rates above 200, not to a particular age.

opts: Correct. Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, and these drugs, like beta blockers and digoxin, cause sinus bradycardia; it would slow her further.
Lisinopril does not slow the sinus node and is not among the listed causes of bradycardia, so it is not the drug to avoid.
A thiazide-type diuretic does not cause sinus bradycardia; the drugs to avoid are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.

Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not nodal reentry.

opts: A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; multifocal atrial tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying illness and signals a poor prognosis.
Correct. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a poor prognostic sign, occurring in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure and right heart stress.
Benign describes focal atrial tachycardia; multifocal atrial tachycardia signals serious underlying illness.

opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with at least three P-wave shapes; an identical abnormal P wave before every QRS in a regular rhythm comes from a single focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

opts: Observation suits pauses that cause no symptoms; ventricular tachycardia alternating with pauses needs a pacemaker with a defibrillator.
Ablation does not fix the failing sinus node behind the pauses; the device answer is a pacemaker with a defibrillator.

Which is the most important treatment for this rhythm?
opts: Correct. Management of multifocal atrial tachycardia is treating the underlying condition, here the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation; short-term rate control may be added in hospital.
Cardioversion does not stop several independent atrial foci; treating the underlying lung disease does.

opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia arises in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure; premature atrial beats in heart disease may precede atrial fibrillation or flutter.
Complete heart block is a failure of conduction to the ventricles, not something premature atrial beats lead to; in heart disease they may precede atrial fibrillation or flutter.

Correct. In patients with heart disease, premature atrial contractions may precede paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, and frequent ones prompt a search for structural heart disease.
Ventricular fibrillation is a ventricular arrest rhythm, not the sequel of premature atrial beats; in a diseased heart they may precede atrial fibrillation, flutter or supraventricular tachycardia.
